Cautiously accommodative tone. The FOMC cut the target range to 1.50–1.75% and added T‑bill purchases and repo operations to maintain ample reserves, signaling support for continued expansion amid weak business fixed investment and soft exports with inflation below 2%. This policy response aligns with stabilization guidance in the literature: New Keynesian evidence (Galí, Gertler, and López-Salido) emphasizes easing when inflation is below target and the output gap widens; empirical work (B. Friedman; Sims, 1992) and structural analyses (McCallum and Nelson, 1999) document that monetary policy has real effects in the short run; and Svensson’s arguments for optimal stabilization under demand shocks support precautionary easing. Given market-based inflation compensation is low, lowering rates helps reduce real rates and support spending and investment, consistent with standard investment and consumption channels in the business-cycle literature. At the same time, the statement’s emphasis on “uncertainties” and persistent weakness in business fixed investment—often a key contributor to cyclical GDP slowdowns—tempers the outlook. Overall, this is a modestly positive, risk-aware stance rather than an unequivocally upbeat one.
